en: Theravāda Vinayapiṭaka Mahāvagga 4.
Pavāraṇā-kkhandhaka (The Chapter on the Invitation)
1. Unpleasant Dwelling.
At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Now at that time, a number of monks who were friends and companions entered the rains retreat together in a certain residence in the Kosala country.
Then it occurred to those bhikkhus:
"By what means might we dwell together in harmony, in mutual agreement, without dispute, comfortably during the rains, and without being exhausted by the search for alms?
Then it occurred to those bhikkhus:
“If we were neither to address nor converse with one another,
then whoever returns first from the village for alms should prepare a seat,
set out water for washing the feet, a footstool, and a foot-washing stone, wash and set out the bowl for refuse, and provide drinking water and water for rinsing the mouth.

If anyone should return from the village for alms later on, and if there is food remaining from his meal, he may eat it if he so desires; if he does not desire to eat it, he should discard it where there is little vegetation or throw it into water that contains no living beings.

He should then put away his seat, put away the foot-stool, the foot-stand, and the foot-washing stone; having washed the bowl for scraps, he should put it away; he should put away the drinking water and the water for washing; and he should sweep the dining hall.
If one should see a water jar, a jar for drinking, or a toilet jar that is empty and void, one should set it out.
If it is too heavy to be carried alone, one should call a second person by a gesture of the hand and set it out by passing it hand to hand;
however, one should not utter a word on that account.
"In this way, being united, harmonious, and without dispute, we shall dwell comfortably during the rains retreat and not be distressed for lack of almsfood.
Then those bhikkhus neither addressed nor conversed with one another.
Whoever returned first from the village for alms would prepare a seat, set out water for washing the feet, and a footstool.
He sets out a foot-stool, washes and prepares a bowl for refuse, and provides drinking water and water for washing.

When he returns from the village on his alms round, if there is food left over from the meal, the attendant eats it if he wishes; if he does not wish to eat it, he discards it where there is no greenery or throws it into water that contains no living beings.

He puts away the seat; he puts away the water for washing the feet, the footstool, and the foot-wiping cloth; having washed the bowl for leftover food, he puts it away; he puts away the drinking water and the water for washing; he sweeps the dining hall.
Whoever sees that the water jar for drinking, the water jar for washing, or the chamber-pot is empty and void, he refills it.
If it is too heavy for him to lift, he calls a companion by a gesture of the hand and refills it by passing it from hand to hand; yet he does not utter a word on that account.
Now it is the custom for monks who have completed the rains retreat to approach the Blessed One to see him.
Then those monks, having completed the rains retreat at the end of the three months, put their lodgings in order and, taking their bowls and robes, set out for Sāvatthī.

Traveling by stages, they arrived at Sāvatthī, at Jetavana, the monastery of Anāthapiṇḍika, and approached the Blessed One. Having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, they sat down to one side.
Now it is the custom for the Blessed Buddhas to exchange greetings with visiting monks.
Then the Blessed One said to those monks:
"I hope, monks, that you are bearing up; I hope you are getting by."
“I hope you have spent the rains comfortably, living in harmony, in mutual appreciation, and without dispute; and that you have not been distressed for lack of almsfood?
“It is bearable, Blessed One; it is sustainable, Blessed One.
We have spent the rains comfortably, living in harmony, in mutual appreciation, and without dispute, and we have not been distressed for lack of almsfood.”
Tathāgatas ask even though they know; they do not ask even though they know.
Having discerned the right time, they ask; having discerned the right time, they do not ask.
Tathāgatas ask what is connected with the goal, not what is unconnected with the goal.
The destruction of the bridge by the Tathāgatas pertains to what is unbeneficial.
Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, question the bhikkhus in two ways: “Shall we teach the Dhamma? or “Shall we lay down a training rule for the disciples?

Then the Blessed One said to those bhikkhus: “But how, bhikkhus, did you spend the rains residence in harmony, in mutual affection, without dispute, living at ease and not distressed for lack of almsfood?”
“Here, Bhante, a number of us—monks who were friends and companions—entered the rains retreat together in a certain monastery in the Kosala country.
Then, Bhante, this thought occurred to us:
‘By what means might we dwell the rains retreat in comfort, living together in harmony, in mutual appreciation, and without dispute, and without being exhausted by the search for alms?’”
"Venerable sir, it occurred to us:
‘If we were neither to address nor converse with one another,
then whoever returns first from the village for alms should prepare a seat, water for washing the feet, and a footstool.’”
He should set out a foot-stool, wash and place out a bowl for refuse, and provide drinking water and water for washing.

When he returns from the village on his alms round, if there is food left over from his meal and if he so desires, he may eat it; if he does not desire it, he should discard it where there is no greenery or throw it into water that contains no living beings.

He should put away the seat; he should put away the water for washing the feet, the footstool, and the foot-wiping cloth; having washed the bowl for leftover food, he should put it away; he should put away the drinking water and the water for washing; he should sweep the dining hall.
Whoever sees that the water jar for drinking, the water jar for washing, or the chamber-pot is empty and void should refill it;
if it is too heavy for him to lift, he should call a companion by a gesture of the hand and refill it by passing it from hand to hand.
Yet we did not, on that account, break out into speech, thinking:
‘In this way we shall dwell together in harmony, in mutual appreciation, without dispute, spending the rains comfortably and not being distressed for lack of almsfood.
Thus, venerable sir, we neither addressed one another nor conversed with one another.
Whoever returns first from the village for alms prepares a seat, sets out water for washing the feet, a footstool, and a foot-washing stone;
having washed the alms-bowl, he sets it aside, and provides drinking water and water for rinsing.
Whoever returns later from the village for alms, if there is food remaining from the meal, eats it if he so desires.
If he does not wish to do so, he discards it in a place free from greenery or casts it into water where there are no living beings.
He puts away his seat, puts away the foot-stool, the foot-stand, and the foot-washing stone; having washed the bowl for refuse, he puts it away;
he puts away the drinking water and the water for washing; and he sweeps the dining hall.
“Whoever sees that the water-jar, the washing-water jar, or the toilet-water jar is empty or depleted refills it.
If it is too heavy for him to carry alone, he calls to a second person with a gesture of the hand and refills it by passing it between them; yet he does not utter a word on that account.
It was in this way, venerable sir, that we lived the rains retreat in harmony, in mutual affection, without dispute, living comfortably and not being distressed for lack of almsfood.”
Then the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus:
“Indeed, bhikkhus, when these foolish men have emerged from a state of discomfort, they claim, ‘We have emerged from a state of comfort.
Indeed, bhikkhus, when these foolish men have emerged from living like cattle, they claim, ‘We have emerged from a state of comfort.’”
"It seems, monks, that when these foolish men have emerged from living like goats, they claim, 'We have emerged in comfort.
It seems, monks, that when these foolish men have emerged from living like enemies, they claim, 'We have emerged in comfort.
How, monks, can these foolish men adopt the vow of silence, the practice of the sectarians?"
“Monks, this does not lead to the confidence of those without confidence...
Having rebuked him and given a discourse on the Dhamma, he addressed the monks:
‘Monks, the practice of the vow of silence undertaken by the monastics of other sects must not be adopted.’”
Whoever should undertake [this] commits an offense of wrong-doing.
Monks, I allow those monks who have completed the rains residence to perform the invitation ceremony (*pavāraṇā*) on three grounds:
by what has been seen, or by what has been heard, or by suspicion.
This will be for you a state of mutual conformity, a rising above offenses, and a priority for the Vinaya.
And furthermore, monks, you should invite criticism in this way:
A learned and competent monk should inform the Saṅgha:
‘Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me.
Today is the Pavāraṇā.
If it seems appropriate to the Saṅgha, let the Saṅgha perform the Pavāraṇā.’”
The senior bhikkhu, having arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, having sat down on his haunches, and having raised his joined palms, should address him thus:
"Friends, I invite the Saṅgha regarding what has been seen, heard, or suspected.
May the venerable ones speak to me out of compassion."
Reflecting, I shall make amends.
A second time, friends, I invite the Saṅgha regarding what has been seen, heard, or suspected.
May the Venerable Ones speak to me out of compassion.
"Reflecting, I shall make amends.
A third time also, friends, I invite the Saṅgha regarding what has been seen, heard, or suspected.
May the Venerable Ones speak to me out of compassion."
‘While reflecting, I shall make amends.
A newly ordained bhikkhu, having arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, having sat down on his haunches, and having extended his hands in añjali, should speak to him thus:
‘Venerable sir, I invite the Saṅgha regarding what has been seen, heard, or suspected.’”
"Let the venerable ones speak to me out of compassion.
Seeing [my fault], I shall make amends.
For a second time, venerable sirs, I appeal to the Saṅgha... [and so on].
For a third time, venerable sirs, I invite the Saṅgha regarding what has been seen, heard, or suspected.
May the venerable ones speak to me out of compassion;
seeing [the fault], I shall make amends.”
Now at that time, while the elder monks were sitting in the *ukkuṭika* posture and performing the invitation ceremony (*pavāraṇā*), the group of six monks remained seated on their chairs.
Those monks who were of few desires... [and so forth]... complained, grumbled, and became indignant, saying:
"How can the group of six monks remain seated on their chairs while the elder monks are sitting in the *ukkuṭika* posture and performing the invitation ceremony?"
Then those bhikkhus reported this matter to the Blessed One...
[as before] ...“Is it true, bhikkhus, that the group-of-six bhikkhus remain on their seats while the elder bhikkhus are sitting in the *ukkuṭika* posture and inviting [them to eat]?
“It is true, Blessed One.”
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked them:
“… How can those foolish men, monks, remain seated on their seats while the elder monks are sitting in the *ukkhuṭika* posture (on their haunches) and inviting [them to speak]?
This, monks, is neither for the inspiration of those without faith nor for the increase of those with faith…” [and so forth].
Having rebuked them … and having given a discourse on the Dhamma, he addressed the monks:
“Monks, one should not remain seated while the elder monks are sitting in the kneeling posture and inviting [one another].”
Whoever should sit otherwise commits an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
“I allow you, monks, for all to perform the invitation ceremony while sitting in the squatting posture.
Now at that time, a certain elder, weak from old age, fell down in a faint while waiting, sitting in the squatting posture until everyone had performed the invitation ceremony.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“I allow you, monks, to remain squatting in that interval until one invites [for criticism], and having invited, to sit on a seat.
2. The Breach of the Invitation (Pavāraṇābheda).
Then it occurred to the bhikkhus,
"How many kinds of invitation (pavāraṇā) are there?
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, there are these two *pavāraṇā* ceremonies:
that on the fourteenth day and that on the fifteenth day. These, monks, are the two *pavāraṇā* ceremonies.”
Then it occurred to the monks:
"How many kinds of *pavāraṇā* formal acts are there?
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.

“Bhikkhus, there are these four kinds of *pavāraṇā* formal acts: a *pavāraṇā* formal act that is contrary to the Dhamma and performed by an incomplete assembly; a *pavāraṇā* formal act that is contrary to the Dhamma but performed by a complete assembly; [a *pavāraṇā* formal act that is according to the Dhamma but performed by an incomplete assembly;
and a *pavāraṇā* formal act that is according to the Dhamma and performed by a complete assembly.]”
A factional invitation ceremony that is contrary to the Dhamma, and a united invitation ceremony that is in accordance with the Dhamma.
In this regard, monks, as for that factional invitation ceremony which is contrary to the Dhamma: such an invitation ceremony, monks, should not be performed.
Nor have I authorized such a formal act of invitation (*pavāraṇākamma*).
In this regard, monks, as for that formal act of invitation which is performed by a unanimous assembly contrary to the Dhamma: monks, such a formal act of invitation must not be performed;
nor have I authorized such a formal act of invitation.
In this regard, monks, as for that which is a *pavāraṇā* legal act that is contrary to the Dhamma and performed by a divided assembly: such a *pavāraṇā* legal act, monks, should not be performed;
nor has such a *pavāraṇā* legal act been authorized by me.
In this regard, monks, as for that which is a *pavāraṇā* legal act that is in accordance with the Dhamma and performed by a united assembly: such a *pavāraṇā* legal act, monks, should be performed.
"And such a procedure for the invitation ceremony (*pavāraṇā*) has been authorized by me.

Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus: 'We shall perform such a procedure for the invitation ceremony, namely, one that is in accordance with the Dhamma and performed by a united assembly.
3. Authorization for Granting the Invitation Ceremony.
Then the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus:
“Assemble, bhikkhus; the Saṅgha will perform the Pavāraṇā ceremony.”
When this was said, a certain bhikkhu said to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, there is a bhikkhu who is ill; he has not come.
“Bhikkhus, I allow an ill bhikkhu to give his invitation.”
And furthermore, monks, it should be given in this way:

that sick monk, having approached another monk, having arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, having sat down on his haunches, and having extended his hands in reverential salutation, should speak thus:

“I give my invitation; take my invitation; announce my invitation; invite on my behalf. If he makes this known by body, or makes it known by speech, or makes it known by both body and speech, the invitation is considered given.
If he does not make it known by body, nor by speech, nor by both body and speech, the invitation has not been given.
If this can be managed, that is good.
If it cannot be managed, then, monks, that sick monk should be brought into the midst of the Saṅgha on a bed or a chair, and the invitation should be performed.
“Monks, if it occurs to the monks who are attending to the sick:
‘If we move the sick person from his place, either his illness will increase or he will pass away,’ then, monks, the sick monk must not be moved from his place.
The Saṅgha should go there and perform the invitation ceremony (pavāraṇā).”
But the Saṅgha must not perform the invitation ceremony with an incomplete assembly.
If it should do so, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
Monks, if the one who conveys the invitation departs from that very place after the invitation has been given, the invitation must be given to another.
If, monks, the bearer of the invitation, after the invitation has been given, renounces the training right there...
or dies... or declares himself a novice... [etc.]... [then the invitation is considered not given].
One who has renounced the training admits it;
one who has committed an ultimate offense admits it;
one who is insane admits it.
One who admits while deranged...
one who admits while overwhelmed by pain...
one who admits while suspended for not seeing an offense...
He admits to having been suspended for not making amends for an offense...
he admits to having been suspended for not relinquishing a pernicious view...
he admits to being a paṇḍaka.
One who lives in communion by theft acknowledges it...
one who has gone over to another sect acknowledges it...
one who is an animal acknowledges it...
One confesses to being a matricide… one confesses to being a patricide… one confesses to being a murderer of an arahant…
One who admits to being a defiler of a bhikkhunī … one who admits to being a schismatic of the Saṅgha … one who admits to having caused the shedding of blood …
If one who possesses both sexual organs claims to be such, the invitation must be given to another.
Monks, if the bearer of the invitation, after the invitation has been given, departs on the way, the invitation remains un-delivered.
Monks, if the bearer of the invitation, after the invitation has been given, renounces the training on the way... [and so forth].
He dies; he confesses to being a novice monk;
he confesses to having renounced the training.
One who has committed the final offense admits it;
one who is insane admits it;
one whose mind is deranged admits it.
One who is obsessed by feeling admits [it]...
one who has been suspended for not seeing an offense admits [it]...
one who has been suspended for not making amends for an offense admits [it].
He confesses that he has been suspended for not relinquishing a wrong view;
he confesses that he is a paṇḍaka;
he confesses that he is one who lives in the community by theft.
One who claims to have gone over to another sect...
one who claims to be an animal...
one who claims to be a matricide...
One confesses to being a patricide… one confesses to being a murderer of an arahant… one confesses to being a defiler of a bhikkhunī…
If one confesses to being a schismatic of the Saṅgha … if one confesses to being a shedder of blood … if one confesses to being a hermaphrodite,
the invitation is not brought forward.
"Monks, if the bearer of the invitation, having been given the invitation, departs after reaching the Saṅgha, the invitation is considered brought.
Monks, if the bearer of the invitation, having been given the invitation, after reaching the Saṅgha,
renounces the training … [or] dies …"
If he admits to being a novice monk...
if he admits to having renounced the training...
if he admits to having committed an offense involving defeat...
He confesses while claiming to be insane;
he confesses while claiming to be deranged;
he confesses while claiming to be overwhelmed by pain.
One who has been suspended for not recognizing an offense acknowledges it;
one who has been suspended for not making amends for an offense acknowledges it;
one who has been suspended for not relinquishing a pernicious view acknowledges it.
One who confesses to being a paṇḍaka...
one who confesses to being a thief-living-in-the-saṅgha...
one who confesses to having gone over to another sect...
One confesses to being an animal...
one confesses to being a matricide...
one confesses to being a patricide...
One who admits to being an assassin of an arahant...
one who admits to being a defiler of a bhikkhunī...
one who admits to being a schismatic of the Saṅgha...
If one who admits to being a shedder of blood...
or one who admits to being a hermaphrodite [is sent], the invitation has been brought.
Monks, if the bearer of the invitation, having been given the invitation, arrives at the Saṅgha while asleep and does not announce it, the invitation has been brought.
There is no offense for the one who conveys the invitation.
Monks, if the conveyor of the invitation, having been given the invitation, reaches the Saṅgha but, being negligent, does not announce it...
[or] if he does not announce it while absorbed in meditation, the invitation is considered conveyed.
There is no offense for the one who brings the invitation.
But if, monks, the one who brings the invitation, having received the invitation, intentionally fails to announce it upon arriving at the Saṅgha, the invitation is considered brought;
there is an offense of wrong-doing for the one who brings the invitation.
“I allow you, monks, on the day of the Pavāraṇā ceremony, when one is granting the Pavāraṇā, to also give consent (*chanda*), if there is business to be done for the Saṅgha.
Now at that time, on the day of the Pavāraṇā, certain relatives seized a certain monk.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One:
“In this case, monks, on the day of the invitation ceremony (*pavāraṇā*), relatives take hold of a monk.
Those relatives should be addressed by the monks in this way:”
‘Please, venerable sirs, release this bhikkhu for a moment, until this bhikkhu has performed the invitation ceremony.
If they can be persuaded to do so, that is good.
If they cannot be persuaded, those bhikkhus should be addressed by the relatives as follows:
‘Please, venerable sirs, stay aside for a moment until this bhikkhu has given his invitation.
If they can do so, that is good.
If they cannot, those bhikkhus should be addressed by the monks as follows:
‘Come now, venerable sirs, lead this bhikkhu outside the boundary for a moment, until the Saṅgha has performed the Pavāraṇā.
If they can do so, that is good.
If they cannot, the Saṅgha must not perform the Pavāraṇā in an incomplete assembly.
If he should invite [the Saṅgha] to the invitation ceremony, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
But here, monks, on the day of the invitation ceremony, kings seize a monk … thieves seize him … [and so forth].
Scoundrels seize them… enemies of the bhikkhus seize them.
Those enemies of the bhikkhus should be addressed by the bhikkhus as follows:
‘Please, venerable sirs, release this bhikkhu for a moment, until this bhikkhu has finished the invitation ceremony.
If they should grant this, it is well.
If they do not grant it, those bhikkhus who are opponents of the bhikkhu should be addressed by the other bhikkhus as follows:
‘Please, venerable sirs, stand aside for a moment until this bhikkhu has given his invitation.
If they can do so, that is good.
If they cannot, those bhikkhus who are adversaries of the bhikkhus should be addressed by the bhikkhus as follows:
‘Come now, venerable sirs, lead this bhikkhu outside the boundary for a moment, until the Saṅgha has performed the Pavāraṇā.
If they can manage it thus, that is good.
If they cannot manage it, the Pavāraṇā must not be performed by an incomplete Saṅgha.
“If one should invite [the Sangha] in this manner, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
Now at that time, on the day of the invitation ceremony (pavāraṇā), five monks were staying in a certain residence.
Then it occurred to those bhikkhus:
"The Blessed One has prescribed:
'The Saṅgha should perform the Pavāraṇā ceremony.'"
“We are five people.
How, indeed, should we perform the invitation ceremony?
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“I allow you, monks, to perform the Pavāraṇā ceremony before a Saṅgha of five.
Now at that time, four monks were staying in a certain residence on the day of Pavāraṇā.
Then it occurred to those monks:
“The Blessed One has authorized the invitation ceremony (*pavāraṇā*) for five in the Saṅgha.
Yet we are only four people.
How, then, should we perform the invitation ceremony?”
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“I allow you, monks, for four [monks] to invite one another.
And thus, monks, should they invite:”
A competent monk who has mastered the procedure should inform those monks:
“Venerable sirs, listen to me.
Today is the invitation ceremony.”
‘If it seems appropriate to the venerable ones, let us invite one another.
The senior bhikkhu, having arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, having sat down on his haunches, and having raised his joined palms in salutation, should address those bhikkhus thus:
‘Friends, I invite the venerable ones regarding what has been seen, heard, or suspected.
"May the venerable ones speak to me out of compassion.
Seeing [my fault], I shall make amends.
A second time... [and so on].
"A third time also, friends, I invite the Venerable Ones regarding what has been seen, heard, or suspected.
May the Venerable Ones speak to me out of compassion;
seeing [my fault], I shall make amends."

The newly ordained bhikkhu, having arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, having sat down on his heels, and having extended his hands in reverential salutation, should address those bhikkhus thus:
"Venerable sirs, I invite the venerable ones regarding what has been seen, heard, or suspected.
May the venerable ones speak to me out of compassion."
"Observing, I shall make amends.
A second time...
and a third time, venerable sir, I invite the venerable ones regarding what has been seen, heard, or suspected.
“Let the venerable ones speak to me out of compassion;
seeing [my fault], I will make amends.
Now at that time, on the day of the Pavāraṇā ceremony, three bhikkhus were staying in a certain residence.
Then it occurred to those bhikkhus:
"The Blessed One has permitted the *pavāraṇā* ceremony to be performed by five in the Saṅgha, or by four among themselves.
We, however, are three persons."
“How, indeed, should we perform the invitation ceremony?
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, I allow three to perform the invitation ceremony with one another.”
And furthermore, monks, the invitation should be performed in this way:
A competent and capable monk should inform those monks:
"Venerable sirs, may you listen to me."
"Today is the invitation ceremony (pavāraṇā).
If it seems appropriate to the Venerable Ones, let us invite one another.
Then the elder bhikkhu, having arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, having sat down on his haunches, and having raised his joined palms in salutation, should address those bhikkhus thus:
“Friends, I invite the Venerable Ones regarding what has been seen, heard, or suspected.
May the Venerable Ones speak to me out of compassion;
seeing [my fault], I shall make amends.”
For a second time...
and for a third time, friends, I invite the Venerable Ones to speak to me regarding what has been seen, heard, or suspected.
May the Venerable Ones speak to me out of compassion.
‘Having seen it, I shall make amends.
A newly ordained bhikkhu, having arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, having sat down on his haunches, and having raised his joined palms in salutation, should address those bhikkhus thus:
‘Venerable sirs, I invite the venerable ones regarding what has been seen, heard, or suspected. May they speak to me out of compassion.’”
"May the venerable ones speak to me out of compassion.
Seeing [my fault], I shall make amends.
A second time... [and so on]...
“Venerable sirs, for a third time I invite the venerable ones regarding what has been seen, heard, or suspected.
May the venerable ones speak to me out of compassion;
seeing it, I shall make amends.”
Now at that time, on the day of the Pavāraṇā ceremony, two bhikkhus were staying in a certain residence.
Then it occurred to those bhikkhus:
"The Blessed One has permitted five [bhikkhus] to perform the Pavāraṇā in the Saṅgha, four to perform the Pavāraṇā with one another, and three to perform the Pavāraṇā with one another."
“We are two people.
How, indeed, should we perform the Pavāraṇā ceremony?
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, I allow two [monks] to invite one another.
And thus, monks, should they invite:
The elder monk, having arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, having sat down on his haunches, and having raised his joined palms, should speak thus to the junior monk:”
“Friends, I invite the Venerable One regarding what has been seen, heard, or suspected.
May the Venerable One speak to me out of compassion;
if I see [the fault], I will make amends.”
A second time...
and a third time, friends, I invite the Venerable One regarding what has been seen, heard, or suspected.
May the Venerable One speak to me out of compassion.

"Thinking, 'I shall confess,' the newly ordained bhikkhu should arrange his upper robe over one shoulder, sit in the kneeling position, raise his joined palms, and address the elder bhikkhu thus: 'Venerable sir,
I invite the Venerable One regarding what has been seen, heard, or suspected.'"
"May the Venerable One speak to me out of compassion;
seeing [my fault], I shall make amends.
A second time... [and so on]...
“Venerable sir, for a third time I invite the Venerable One regarding what has been seen, heard, or suspected.
May the Venerable One speak to me out of compassion;
if I see [the fault], I will make amends.”
Now at that time, on the day of the invitation ceremony (*pavāraṇā*), a certain monk was staying alone in a particular monastery.
Then it occurred to that monk:

"The Blessed One has authorized the invitation ceremony to be performed within a Saṅgha of five, to be performed mutually by four, to be performed mutually by three, and to be performed mutually by two."
"I am all alone.
How, indeed, should I perform the invitation ceremony?
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.

Let the venerable Saṅgha hear me.
"While we have been dwelling together in harmony, in mutual agreement, and without dispute, a certain state of well-being has been attained.
If we were to perform the invitation ceremony now, it is possible that the monks, having performed the invitation, might depart on tour;
in this way, we would be excluded from this state of well-being."

The Saṅgha performs a suspension of the invitation ceremony (*pavāraṇā-saṅgaha*); it will now perform the Uposatha and recite the Pātimokkha. On the coming full moon of the Komudī Cātumāsī, it will perform the invitation ceremony.

Whichever venerable one approves of performing the suspension of the invitation ceremony—so that it will now perform the Uposatha, recite the Pātimokkha, and perform the invitation ceremony on the coming full moon of the Komudī Cātumāsī—let him be silent;
whoever does not approve, let him speak.
“The Saṅgha has postponed the invitation ceremony; now it will perform the Uposatha and recite the Pātimokkha. It will invite [at the end of] the fourth month on the full moon of Kattika (Komudī).
This is agreeable to the Saṅgha; therefore, by silence, I hold it so.
If, monks, after those monks have postponed the invitation ceremony, another monk should speak thus:
‘Friend, I wish to set out on a journey through the countryside;
I have business to attend to in the countryside,’ he should be told:
‘Very well, friend, go after you have invited [the Sangha] to a meal.’
If, monks, while a monk is performing the invitation ceremony (*pavāraṇā*), he suspends the invitation of another monk, that monk should be addressed thus:
"Friend, you have no authority over my invitation; I will not perform the invitation yet.
If, monks, while that monk is performing the invitation, another monk suspends his invitation, both must be examined and interrogated by the Saṅgha and then dealt with according to the Dhamma.
If, monks, a monk, having settled his business in the countryside, returns again to that residence within the four-month period of the Komudī full moon,
and while those monks are performing the invitation ceremony (*pavāraṇā*),
another monk cancels that monk’s invitation, he should be addressed thus:
‘Friend, you are not independent regarding my invitation;
I have already been invited.
If, while those monks are being invited, that monk [prevents] the invitation of another monk...
"Having set them aside, and having both been examined and interrogated by the Saṅgha, and having had them dealt with according to the Dhamma, the Saṅgha should perform the Pavāraṇā ceremony.
